name: Ambergris

lead: Ambergris is a waxy, flammable material produced in the digestive system of sperm whales and found floating at sea or washed ashore. Aged pieces smell sweet and earthy, and perfumers have prized them as a fixative that helps a fragrance last longer on skin.

For looks and grooming, the payoff is scent: a longer-lasting, smoother fragrance contributes to the impression a person makes. Today the characteristic note comes mostly from synthetic ambroxide, and research on ambergris is mainly chemistry and biosynthesis.

paras: In practice people meet ambergris as a note or ingredient in niche perfumes, or as ambroxide-based fragrances. It is worn like any fragrance, on skin and clothes, and is often layered with other scents.
Natural ambergris trade is prohibited in the US under the Endangered Species Act, while it is legal in the UK and EU. Fragrance ingredients can cause skin sensitivity in some people.

chain: A more lasting, polished scent impression
angle.text: Worn as part of a perfume, ambergris or ambroxide gives fragrances a warm, lasting base. People who care about how they smell choose such perfumes for longevity.

lead: Ambergris is a waxy solid produced by sperm whales. It is rare, thought to be produced by about one percent of whales, and is usually found floating or on shores.[1] Fresh pieces smell marine; with ageing it becomes sweet and earthy.[1]

In perfumery it is valued as a fixative: it slows evaporation of other fragrance materials so a scent lasts longer on the skin.[1] This is how it relates to appearance, since fragrance is part of grooming and personal presentation.

Its main component, ambrein, is odourless; oxidation produces ambroxide and related odour compounds.[2][3] The fragrance industry now relies largely on synthetic or semisynthetic ambroxide made from plant precursors such as sclareol from clary sage.[3][4]
infobox: Trade prohibited in US; legal in UK and EU

paras: Ambergris contains roughly 25–45 percent of the triterpenoid ambrein and 40–46 percent cholestanol-type steroids.[3] Environmental oxidation of ambrein produces odorous compounds including ambroxide, also sold as Ambrox.[3][1]
Ambrein was identified in 1946 by Ružička and Lardon.[1]

Perfumers have used ambergris as a fixative and scent note.[1] Because supply is scarce and legal status uncertain in some regions, manufacturers moved to synthetics; ambroxide is now widely used.[4][1] Reviews describe the fragrance industry as using ambrafuran materials entirely from synthetic or semisynthetic sources.[3]
Ancient Egyptians burned it as incense, and medieval Europeans used it as a remedy; it also flavoured foods and drinks historically.[1]

Large finds make news; a 127 kg piece found off Yemen in 2021 was valued at about US$1.5 million.[1] Trade is prohibited in the US under the Endangered Species Act, legal in the UK and EU, and restricted in Australia and India.[1]
Reviews describe microbial biosynthesis of ambrein and ambroxide from sugars and glycerol, and enzymatic routes from plant diterpenes, as sustainable alternatives to whale-derived material.[2][4]
No studies found. Published research concerns the chemistry and sustainable production of ambergris-type fragrance compounds, not their effect on appearance.
